summary.brief: The presenter demonstrates how to tape the knob of a hockey stick using a half roll of tape and a candy‑cane wrap.
summary.detailed: The video opens with the presenter listing the needed items—a roll of tape (any colour), scissors (optional), and a hockey stick. He tears the roll in half and uses the half‑roll to create a tight “candy‑cane” spiral along the shaft, pulling the tape off the roll and wrapping it upward with the turns placed close together. After covering the desired length of the shaft, he cuts a short length of tape, places it at the end of the stick (the knob), and spirals it around the knob several times, squeezing the layers together to form a solid coil. He trims any excess and shows the finished, neatly wrapped knob.

action.brief: Tape the knob of a hockey stick
action.detailed: Pull a length of tape from a half roll, wrap it in a tight candy‑cane spiral up the shaft, cut a short piece, and wind that piece tightly around the knob while squeezing the layers together, then trim any excess.
action.actor: A presenter wearing a blue hoodie who holds the hockey stick in his hands

summary.brief: A man in a Chicago hoodie tapes the knob of a hockey stick.
summary.detailed: The video opens with only the torso and arms of a man wearing a dark‑blue Chicago sweatshirt visible. He grabs a roll of tape, rips it in half, and holds a pair of scissors. Starting near the top of the stick he wraps the tape in a candy‑cane style, pulling the strip tight, overlapping the layers while rotating the stick, and then cuts off the excess. He then moves down the shaft, wrapping the tape around the pole with a few twists and rotating the stick to cover all sides, cutting pieces as needed. Finally he shifts to the knob, winds a smaller amount of tape around it a couple of times, squeezes the layers together to the desired thickness, and trims any remaining excess. The entire procedure is shown in a sped‑up close‑up view against a room with a wooden wall, stairs and a TV.

action.detailed: Pull a piece of tape from the roll, wind it tightly around the stick knob while rotating the stick, compress the layers, and trim the excess with scissors.

He trims any excess, inspects the finished knob, then lifts the stick toward the camera to show the completed taping before the clip ends with him walking out of the frame.

summary_sent_to_llm.root_summary: The video opens with the presenter listing the needed items—a roll of tape (any colour), scissors (optional), and a hockey stick. He tears the roll in half and uses the half‑roll to create a tight “candy‑cane” spiral along the shaft, pulling the tape off the roll and wrapping it upward with the turns placed close together. After covering the desired length of the shaft, he cuts a short length of tape, places it at the end of the stick (the knob), and spirals it around the knob several times, squeezing the layers together to form a solid coil. He trims any excess and shows the finished, neatly wrapped knob.

llm.system_prompt:
You evaluate YouTube videos for a video-understanding benchmark.

You will be given an Action100M-style summary of one video: title, description,
a hierarchical GPT-written summary of the whole video, and a deduplicated list
of action labels extracted at multiple levels of the video.

Your job is to judge:

1) DOMAINS — does this video clearly belong to any of these target domains?
   - "kitchen": a person preparing food in a kitchen-like setting
     (cooking, baking, food prep — NOT eating reviews, NOT pet-food prep,
     NOT food-product unboxing, NOT restaurant vlogs).
   - "manipulation": a person performing hand-object manipulation tasks
     with clear physical goals: assembly/disassembly, repair, crafting,
     tool use, packing, sorting. The video must show clear procedural
     manipulation, NOT just incidental hand movement (e.g. a vlog where
     someone holds things while talking does NOT count).
   - "navigation": the camera moves through a physical environment as an
     agent traverses space — first-person walking tours (museum, store,
     home, city street), driving / cycling / hiking POV footage, drone
     fly-throughs of indoor or outdoor scenes, room/house walkthroughs.
     The camera's translation through the environment IS the main content.
     Does NOT count: a stationary tripod with someone talking; a tutorial
     filmed in one place; b-roll where the camera only pans or zooms but
     does not translate; sports footage where the player moves but the
     camera stays put.
   A video can match zero, one, or multiple domains. Be strict — when in
   doubt, say "neither".

2) NUM_DISTINCT_EVENTS — count the number of *semantically distinct*
   sub-events (procedural steps) you see in the action list. Merge
   paraphrases of the same step into one. Ignore generic narration steps
   like "speak to camera" or "display title".

3) IS_GOOD_CANDIDATE — true only if BOTH:
   - at least one target domain matches
   - num_distinct_events > 3 (the video shows a real multi-step procedure)

Always return strict JSON in the requested schema.
